opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is a good question, and I think it's one where the honest answer is that the data we have doesn't strongly pin it down.

The constant-hazard picture says that as an agent works on a task, there's some roughly fixed chance per unit of time that it makes an unrecoverable mistake. If that's true, success probability falls off exponentially with task length, and you get a natural "half-life" framing: the task length at which the model succeeds half the time. That's a really appealing story. It's simple, it gives you a mechanistic intuition, and it gives you predictions about how success rates at different thresholds, like 50% versus 80%, should relate to each other.

What we did in the paper was fit a logistic curve against the log of how long tasks take humans. That was a fairly pragmatic choice. It's a standard tool from item response theory, it fit the data reasonably well, and we weren't trying to commit to a particular story about why models fail.

Within the range where we have a lot of data, the two models make fairly similar predictions. Both give you a declining success curve, and the 50% point comes out in a similar place. Where they really differ is the tails. Under constant hazard, success on very long tasks drops off quite sharply. The logistic-in-log-time fit has a heavier tail, so it predicts models will occasionally succeed at tasks much longer than their horizon. With our task suite, we just don't have enough very long tasks, or enough runs on them, to distinguish those confidently.

I'd also say I'm a bit skeptical that the hazard is really constant. A lot of what makes long tasks hard isn't a uniform per-minute chance of failure. Some tasks have a single crux that's really difficult. Some failures are recoverable: a good agent notices it went down the wrong path and backs up. That's a big part of what distinguishes skilled humans, and to the extent models get better at error recovery, you'd expect the effective hazard to fall over the course of a task rather than stay flat. Human completion time is also a noisy proxy for how many opportunities to fail a task actually contains.

So my overall take is that constant hazard is a useful first-order model and a nice way to build intuition, and it's a good thing to test against. But I wouldn't treat it as established, and I wouldn't lean much on extrapolations that depend on the exact tail shape. The more robust claim from our work is about the trend: whatever curve you fit, the horizon has been growing quickly and fairly consistently. Distinguishing these functional forms properly would require many more long tasks and more runs per task, and that's something we're interested in.

r001.rationale: It says a roughly fixed failure chance per unit time makes success probability fall exponentially with task length.

r002.rationale: It weighs the simplicity and intuition of constant hazard against the logistic fit, says the available data do not settle the choice, and notes that tasks differ in their failure and recovery patterns.

r003.rationale: It mentions that human completion time is a noisy proxy for opportunities to fail, but does not identify the task’s intrinsic number of required actions as a basis for constant hazard.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because they're really answering different questions, and I think people sometimes conflate them.

The logistic fit in the time-horizon paper is basically a measurement tool. We have a bunch of tasks, each with a human baseline time, and we observe whether a given model succeeds or fails on each one. Then we fit a curve where success probability goes down as a function of log task length, and we read off the point where that curve crosses fifty percent. That's the time horizon. The logistic form is a modeling choice, it's borrowed from item response theory, and it's convenient because it gives you a single scalar per model, a slope parameter, and a reasonably well-behaved thing to track over time. But I don't think anyone on the team would claim the logistic is the true generative story of why models fail.

The constant-hazard explanation is more of a mechanistic hypothesis. The idea is that an agent has some per-step or per-minute probability of making an unrecoverable mistake, and if that probability is roughly constant, then survival over a task of length t falls off exponentially. And what's interesting is that an exponential decay in task length actually looks a lot like a logistic in log task length over the range we care about. So the two are not really in tension empirically, at least not with the data we had. You can fit either and they'll both look okay.

Where I think the constant-hazard story earns its keep is that it makes predictions about shape. If failures were truly a memoryless process, you'd expect the fall-off to be pretty steep in log-space, and you'd expect the fifty percent horizon and the eighty percent horizon to sit at a fixed ratio of each other, something like a factor of ten to fifteen. And that's roughly what we see, which is suggestive. It also gives you a nice intuition for why horizons double rather than grow linearly: if you cut the per-step error rate in half, you double the expected length before failure.

But I'm honestly skeptical that constant hazard is literally right. A few reasons. One, our tasks aren't homogeneous. Longer tasks aren't just more of the same steps, they tend to require more planning, more state tracking, more recovery from earlier mistakes. So the hazard probably isn't constant within a task, it probably increases as context fills up or as the agent gets further from the original plan. Two, a lot of failures we see aren't a random slip at step forty seven. They're the model fundamentally not having a good approach, which is a failure at step zero that only reveals itself later. That's not really a hazard-rate phenomenon. And three, models can recover. Later agents in particular will notice something's broken and fix it, which breaks the "unrecoverable mistake" assumption.

So how I weigh them: the logistic is what I'd actually use to measure and compare models, because it's agnostic and it works. The constant-hazard model is a useful first-order story for explaining why the curve has the shape it does and why the trend is exponential rather than something else. But I'd treat it as a baseline to deviate from rather than a law. If I wanted to test it seriously, I'd want much finer-grained data than pass/fail: where in the trajectory the agent went wrong, whether it noticed, whether failures cluster early or late. That would tell you whether the hazard is flat, and my guess is it's not, and that the deviations from flatness are where a lot of the interesting capability differences between models actually live.

r001.rationale: It says a roughly constant per-step or per-minute chance of unrecoverable error makes survival over task duration fall exponentially.

r002.rationale: It notes that both fits look acceptable and that tasks are heterogeneous, but does not express uncertainty about balancing empirical fit against model simplicity.

r003.rationale: It describes a per-step hazard, but does not identify a task’s intrinsic required number of actions as a basis for the model.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re explanations at somewhat different levels. A constant-hazard model says that, as an agent works through a task, it has some roughly constant chance of making a fatal mistake per unit of work. That gives you exponential decay in success probability as the amount of work increases. It’s a useful baseline: you can get poor performance on long tasks without positing some special inability to plan over long horizons.

The logistic fit is more of a description of how success varies with task length. A good fit doesn’t, by itself, tell you what’s causing the failures. And task length here is measured by how long a human takes, which isn’t necessarily proportional to the number of opportunities the AI has to make a mistake.

So I’d want to compare their predictions on individual tasks, rather than just ask which curve looks better on the aggregate. Does the agent have a similar failure rate throughout a trajectory? Can it recover from mistakes? Do failures concentrate at particular difficult steps? Those observations would help distinguish the mechanisms.

My inclination is to take constant hazard seriously as a baseline, but not treat either model as established by the time-horizon curve alone. The fitted horizon can still be a useful summary even if the mechanism behind it is unresolved.

r001.rationale: It says constant hazard produces exponential decay with amount of work, but does not connect that relationship to human task duration; it instead notes that human duration may not track opportunities for AI mistakes.

r002.rationale: It favors comparing task-level predictions over aggregate curves, but does not express uncertainty about balancing empirical fit against model simplicity when the data aggregate different distributions.

r003.rationale: It refers to work and opportunities to make mistakes, but does not identify the intrinsic number of actions required by a task as a possible basis for the constant-hazard model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are explanations at somewhat different levels. The logistic curve is a way of summarizing the relationship between task length and success probability. A constant-hazard model gives you a possible mechanism: at each step, there’s some chance of making an error that you can’t recover from, so your probability of completing the whole task falls exponentially with its length.

One subtlety is that the logistic fit is against log task duration. Over a limited range, that can look fairly similar to exponential decay in duration. So I wouldn’t take a good logistic fit as strong evidence against a constant-hazard account. You’d want to compare their predictions, especially away from the middle of the curve.

But I also wouldn’t assume the hazard really is constant. Longer tasks can require different capabilities, errors can be correlated, and models can sometimes notice mistakes and recover. And human completion time is only a proxy for how many opportunities the model has to fail. So I’d treat constant hazard as a useful baseline, and the logistic as a useful descriptive fit, without treating either as an established explanation of why agents fail.

r001.rationale: It says a constant per-step unrecoverable-error chance makes completion probability fall exponentially with task length, and identifies human completion time as a proxy for failure opportunities.

r002.rationale: It compares the logistic fit and constant-hazard account, but does not discuss balancing fit against simplicity or data aggregating different distributions.

r003.rationale: It mentions a per-step hazard, but does not identify the task’s intrinsic number of required actions as a basis for that model.
